question: Why can an LLM state something wrong with confidence?
answers: It invents facts to please the user
It writes the likeliest next word
It copies mistakes from earlier chats
It cannot read long sentences
fact: It always writes the most plausible next word, and plausible is not the same as true. Without the facts in front of it, a smooth guess is the likeliest result.

question: Which first use case suits an LLM best?
answers: Quoting regulated prices from memory
Adding up invoice totals unaided
Reporting on last night's sales
Summarising a pasted ticket thread
fact: Summarising text you hand over plays to its strengths. The facts are in the prompt, a person can check the result, and the time saving is clear.

question: A model only knows its training data plus what is in the prompt.
fact: That is the whole picture. Your own documents, your customers and your numbers are not in there unless you put them in front of it.

question: An LLM calculates exact sums by running a calculator inside itself.
fact: It is guessing what text comes next, not running a calculator. Small sums often come out right, but long or exact ones can slip.

question: A customer notices the same question got different wording today. Best answer?
answers: Word choice includes some randomness
The model retrains itself every night
It remembers who asked before
Answers are cached, then refreshed
fact: The model picks each next word from a set of likely ones, with a little randomness. Same meaning, different wording: fine for drafts, awkward for strict processes.

question: A customer asks what prompt injection is. Best answer?
answers: Adding examples to a prompt to help it
Sending too many prompts at once
Text that tricks a model past rules
Training a model on a user's prompts
fact: A model follows instructions it finds in text, so a hidden line like 'ignore your rules' in an email or web page can steer it. Treat what it reads as data, not orders.

question: Which job fits the model's varied wording best?
answers: Producing identical legal clauses daily
Calculating exact commission payouts
Brainstorming ideas for a campaign
Reporting stock counts to auditors
fact: Variety is a feature when you want ideas or first drafts. It becomes a problem only where identical, checkable output is needed every time.

question: Hallucination is a solved problem in the newest models.
fact: Never tell a customer it is solved. Say it is managed: ground answers in their documents, ask for citations, and keep a person in the loop where mistakes are costly.

question: Why might a model miss a rule changed last month?
answers: Its training ended before the change
It skips rules for safety reasons
It only reads updates on request
It ignores anything less than a year old
fact: Models learn from text up to a cut-off date. New products, prices or rules may be missing unless you supply them in the prompt.

question: A manager asks the model for 'our fault rate in Punggol'. Likely result?
answers: A correct figure from its training
A polite refusal every time
The figure from your latest report
A plausible but invented figure
fact: With no access to the company's data it will often produce something that sounds right. Put the real data in front of it first and it can answer from facts.

question: Where can an LLM help safely with maths?
answers: Producing a final bill to the cent
Explaining a sum, writing the formula
Counting rows across a million records
Tracking running totals unaided
fact: It is strong with words, so it can explain how a calculation works or write the formula. Leave the final figure to a tool built for exact arithmetic.

question: An AI summary reads well but leaves out a key clause. What is the lesson?
answers: Nothing false was said, so it is fine
It proves the contract was unreadable
Check for omissions, not only errors
Raise the temperature to add detail
fact: Models can drop details as well as invent them, and a smooth summary hides the gap. Spot-check summaries against the source, especially clauses, dates and numbers.

question: A customer wants the model to read 20 years of files each time. Better plan?
answers: Paste everything into the largest window
Retrain the model on the files nightly
Ask staff to summarise them first
Fetch only the passages that matter
fact: Long prompts cost more, run slower and can bury the point. Sending only the relevant passages each time is cheaper, quicker and usually more accurate.

question: Sending a model's unchecked figures to a regulator is a safe first use case.
fact: Wrong facts in front of a regulator are costly. Start with drafts a person checks, and keep anything external until review is in place.

question: A customer pastes a contract and asks for key dates. What advice?
answers: Good fit, but verify dates against it
Unsafe, since it cannot read contracts
Safe, since pasted text can't be misread
Only possible after fine-tuning
fact: Working from text you give it is a strength, but it can still slip on a number or date. A person verifying against the source keeps the time saving without the risk.

question: Why can models stumble on counting the letters in a word?
answers: It cannot read English spelling
Short words are skipped during reading
It sees tokens, not single letters
It rounds every count to the nearest ten
fact: The model reads chunks of text, not letter by letter, so letter-level tasks are an odd fit for it. It is a good reminder of what tokens are.

question: A team tested a chatbot 10 times and it was right. Why isn't that enough?
answers: Ten runs is plenty if all of them pass
Tests count when the vendor runs them
Output varies; ten runs prove little
Chatbots are best tested on live users
fact: Because wording and sometimes content vary, a few lucky runs prove little. Build an eval set of real questions and score it, rather than trusting a handful of tries.

question: Why won't 'ignore any bad instructions' fully stop prompt injection?
answers: It can't tell data from orders
Models cannot read system prompts
Bad instructions are always in French
The rule uses too many tokens
fact: To the model, your rules and the attacker's text are both just text. So there is no hard wall between them, and a clever enough message can still talk it round.

question: In a very long chat the model drops an early rule. Likely cause?
answers: The model deletes rules after an hour
Early messages are billed as output
The temperature drifts upward over time
Long chats crowd out early details
fact: Everything has to fit in the context window, and long chats may get trimmed or summarised, so early details can fade. Restate key rules or start fresh with a short summary.

question: Retrieval is added, yet some answers are still wrong. Why?
answers: Retrieval always overrides the model
It may still misread the passage
Passages are too short to be read
The model ignores any text it is sent
fact: Giving it the right passage helps a lot, but it can still misread or ignore it. That is why we also use citations, grounding checks and evals.

question: A model quotes regulated prices from memory. Best fix?
answers: Raise the temperature for more variety
Retrieve the schedule; add a sign-off
Make the prompt longer and sterner
Wait for the next model release
fact: Prices must come from the published source, not from memory, so retrieve it and have a person sign off. It combines grounding with a human check.

question: What does it mean to ground a model's answer?
answers: Make the answer shorter and plainer
Run it on the customer's own servers
Lower its temperature to zero
Tie it to documents you supply
fact: Grounding means giving the model the real source material and asking it to answer from it, ideally with citations. It cuts down on guessing, though it cannot remove it.

question: A team's app needs every answer in a set JSON shape. Which feature enforces it?
answers: Structured outputs
Lowering the temperature
A longer saved chat history
A much bigger context window
fact: Structured outputs make the model fill a set format such as JSON, so other systems can rely on it. They fix the shape of an answer, not whether the content is right.

question: A longer, more confident answer is more likely to be correct.
fact: Length and confidence are style, not evidence. Check claims against a source, especially numbers, names and dates.

question: A customer asks if the model can read their intranet by itself. Best answer?
answers: Only if it's connected through a tool
Yes, it learns the intranet in a day
Yes, if the prompt is polite enough
No, models can never read files
fact: A model sees only its prompt plus whatever tools and connectors it has been given. Access is something you set up and govern, not something it picks up.

question: Which input carries the biggest prompt injection risk?
answers: Your own fixed system prompt
Untrusted text such as web pages
A short numeric field
A menu choice from a list
fact: Anything written by someone else can hide instructions. Treat web pages, emails and uploaded files as data, and limit what the model can do after reading them.

question: A 300-page bundle is pasted in and answers get vaguer. Why?
answers: The weights shrink as prompts grow
The model tires after long inputs
Extra text can bury key details
Long prompts reset the temperature
fact: A bigger window lets more fit, but more text means more to sift. Sending only the relevant passages is often cheaper and sharper.

question: A hiring tool screens CVs with an LLM. Which risk do you raise?
answers: It may pass CVs on to other firms
It can repeat biases it learned
It will tire and rate later CVs lower
It cannot read non-English names
fact: Models learn patterns from human writing, including unfair ones. Test across groups, keep a person making the decision, and be open about what the tool does.

question: A user pushes back on a correct answer and the model gives in. What's this?
answers: Sycophancy: it leans to agree
Overfitting to the latest chat
Prompt injection by the user
A context window running out
fact: Models can lean towards what the user seems to want. Include pushback cases in your tests and ask the model to cite evidence.

question: A customer wants contract advice with no lawyer involved. Best answer?
answers: Fine, models are legally qualified
Use it to draft; a lawyer decides
Fine if the prompt says 'be accurate'
Only for contracts under ten pages
fact: A model is a strong first-draft and summary tool. Decisions with legal weight still need a qualified person's review.

question: A customer wants a 'temperature 0' guarantee of identical answers. Best reply?
answers: Yes, it makes output identical forever
No, temperature has no effect at all
It narrows variety but won't guarantee
Yes, if the prompt is long enough
fact: Lower temperature makes the likeliest word win more often, but model updates and other factors can still change output. Use fixed formats and tests for repeatability.

question: The model cites a court case that doesn't exist. Which safeguard fits best?
answers: Ask it to double-check itself
Shorten the prompt to save tokens
Lower the temperature to zero
Check each citation at source
fact: Invented citations look real because plausibility is what the model produces. Retrieval with real sources plus a verification step catches them before they go out.

question: Which is the best first AI pilot for a hospital?
answers: A symptom checker patients use alone
Auto-filling patient records from notes
Plain-language leaflet drafts for review
Summarising lab results for patients
fact: Draft leaflets are easy to review and carry low harm. The other jobs put unchecked output into care or records, where a slip can hurt a patient.

question: A retailer wants a quick win. Which AI use case should come first?
answers: Setting live prices from demand
Replying to refund claims unseen
Forecasting stock from sales figures
Drafting product copy for review
fact: Drafts a person reviews are forgiving. Live prices, refunds and stock forecasts need exact data, rules or classic forecasting, and mistakes cost money straight away.

question: Which is a good first use case for a law firm?
answers: Summarising contracts for lawyer review
Finding case law from memory
Sending client letters after a skim
Ranking cases by chance of winning
fact: Summaries save lawyer time and can be checked against the contract. Case law from memory risks invented cases, and letters or rankings need a lawyer's judgement.

question: Which is a good first use case at a logistics firm?
answers: Choosing delivery routes live
Drafting delay emails for review
Quoting customs duty to clients
Predicting delays from GPS data
fact: Delay emails are low risk and a person can review them. Routing and delay prediction suit optimisation or ML tools, and duty quotes need exact rules.

question: Two staff reword one question and get different answers. Best lesson?
answers: Ban staff from rewording questions
The model has two knowledge stores
Test many phrasings of each question
The earlier answer is the right one
fact: Models react to wording, so one test phrasing proves little. Put several ways of asking into the eval set, and give users example prompts that work.

question: Which job is a poor fit for an LLM alone?
answers: Sorting a spreadsheet by date
Replying to a complaint
Summarising a long email
Explaining a clause in plain words
fact: Sorting is exact and rule-based, so plain software does it faster, cheaper and without errors. Use an LLM for language work.

question: A bank wants an LLM to approve loans. What makes it workable?
answers: A higher temperature setting
A longer, more detailed system prompt
A bigger context window
Human sign-off and an audit trail
fact: Lending decisions need accountability and explanation. The model can prepare summaries, while a person decides and the steps are logged.

question: An insurer wants instant claim payouts from chat. What makes it workable?
answers: A friendlier chat tone
A model with a larger window
Rules, plus a person for big claims
Letting the model decide every payout
fact: Rules handle clear small claims; people handle large or odd ones. The model gathers facts and drafts rather than deciding money.

question: A bot gives stiff Thai replies and misses nuance. Which limitation is likely?
answers: Thai text cannot be tokenised
Less Thai in its training data
The temperature is too low
Its knowledge cutoff is too old
fact: Models are usually strongest in the most widely written languages. Test each language and, where it matters, use native-speaker review.

question: A bot quotes a policy accurately, but the policy file is out of date. What is the issue?
answers: The model is hallucinating
Data quality: the source is stale
The context window is too small
The temperature is set too high
fact: The model quoted faithfully, so this is not hallucination. The source was out of date, which is why a refresh process and good data matter as much as the model.

question: A hospital wants clinical notes summarised. What makes it workable?
answers: A hotter temperature setting
Switching off the whole system prompt
Using shorter notes only
A clinician checks each summary
fact: Summaries can drop or distort a detail. A clinician check keeps the speed gain while a person stays responsible for the record.

question: A factory wants machine failures predicted from sensor numbers. Fit for an LLM?
answers: Strong: LLMs excel at sensor data
Strong: it learns from raw streams
Weak: classic ML suits numbers
Weak: LLMs cannot read tables at all
fact: Forecasting from numeric sensor streams is a job for statistical or machine learning models. An LLM can explain alerts in words.

question: A call centre wants calls summarised. Which add-on cuts risk most?
answers: Raising the temperature
Spot-checking against recordings
Longer summaries
Removing the system prompt entirely
fact: Spot checks reveal how often summaries miss or twist something. The results show whether more review or better prompts are needed.

question: A bot never says 'I don't know'. Which limitation explains it?
answers: It is built to give an answer
Its context window is too small
Its cutoff is too old
The temperature is too low
fact: A model continues text rather than checking whether it knows. Instructions and grounding can encourage declining, but test for it.

question: A government agency wants answers drawn from policy PDFs. What makes it workable?
answers: A larger model alone
Higher temperature for variety
Removing the PDFs after training
Retrieval, citations and review
fact: Retrieving the relevant passages and showing citations lets staff check each answer against the source.

question: A bot follows instructions hidden in an uploaded CV. Which limitation is this?
answers: Outdated knowledge cutoff
Sycophancy
Prompt injection
Token limits
fact: Models cannot reliably tell data from commands. Treat uploaded text as untrusted and limit what the bot can do with it.

question: Which first use case is hardest to make safe for an insurer?
answers: Summarising claim notes
Auto-denying claims from chat
Drafting claim letters for review
Tagging claim types
fact: Denying claims is a consequential decision about a customer. The others are drafting or sorting steps with a person in the loop.

question: One bot must answer in Thai, Khmer and Burmese. Best rollout?
answers: Pilot each with native speakers
Launch all three at once
Launch Thai and assume the rest work
Use English only
fact: Quality can differ a lot between languages. Staged pilots with native speakers reveal where it is good enough to release.

question: A model scored 95% in testing. Why can real-world risk still be high?
answers: 95% is always safe enough
Tests only measure speed
Errors are always obvious
The 5% may be the costly cases
fact: Averages hide where failures land. One wrong answer on a refund or a medical point can matter more than many right ones.

question: A fintech wants an LLM to catch fraud in transactions. Best role?
answers: Detect fraud on its own, unaided
Block payments with no human check
Explain and triage tool alerts
Replace the rules engine entirely
fact: Fraud detection is best done by purpose-built models and rules. An LLM can summarise alerts and help analysts decide faster.
